meta.description: The face of the Earth through backscatter. Mountains, caves, trenches, parks, and natural wonders — every landmark is a measurement the planet made of itself.

nodes.label: MOUNTAINS — The Earth Pushed Upward
nodes.description: Tectonic collision and volcanic eruption frozen in stone. Every mountain is backscatter from a plate boundary.

nodes.label: CAVES — The Earth Hollowed Out
nodes.description: Water dissolved limestone over millions of years. Every cave is negative space — the absence of rock is the measurement.

nodes.label: OCEAN TRENCHES — The Earth Pulled Down
nodes.description: Subduction zones where one plate dives beneath another. The deepest points on Earth — negative elevation, maximum depth.

nodes.label: NATIONAL PARKS — Protected Backscatter
nodes.description: 63 US national parks. Geological, biological, and cultural backscatter that humans decided was worth protecting.

nodes.label: NATURAL WONDERS — Planetary Signatures
nodes.description: The seven natural wonders of the world. Each one a different way the Earth reveals itself.

nodes.label: Mount Everest (Sagarmatha/Chomolungma) — 8,849m — Highest Point on Earth
nodes.description: India collided with Asia 50 million years ago. The collision is still happening. Everest rises 1cm/year. First ascent: Hillary & Tenzing, 1953. The mountain is the backscatter of continental collision — the Earth's surface recording the force of two plates that cannot pass through each other.

nodes.label: K2 (Chhogori) — 8,611m — The Savage Mountain
nodes.description: Second highest, but far deadlier than Everest. 1 death for every 4 summits. The Karakoram is younger, steeper, more violent than the Himalayas. K2's backscatter says: the Earth is still angry here.

nodes.label: Kangchenjunga — 8,586m — Five Treasures of Snows
nodes.description: Third highest. Sacred to the Lepcha and Limbu peoples. Climbers traditionally stop short of the true summit out of respect. The mountain's backscatter includes human reverence — not just geology.

nodes.label: Lhotse — 8,516m — South Peak of Everest
nodes.description: Fourth highest. Connected to Everest by the South Col. Same collision, same plate boundary, different peak. Geological siblings.

nodes.label: Makalu — 8,485m — The Great Black
nodes.description: Fifth highest. A perfect pyramid. 22km SE of Everest. Isolated, steep, technically demanding.

nodes.label: Aconcagua — 6,962m — Highest in Americas & Southern Hemisphere
nodes.description: Not volcanic — pushed up by subduction of the Nazca Plate beneath South America. The Andes are the longest continental mountain range on Earth (7,000 km). Aconcagua is their crown.

nodes.label: Denali (Mt. McKinley) — 6,190m — Highest in North America
nodes.description: Highest base-to-peak rise of any mountain on Earth's surface (~5,500m from base). The Alaska Range formed from Pacific Plate subduction. Denali National Park: 6 million acres of wilderness.

nodes.label: Kilimanjaro (Uhuru Peak) — 5,895m — Highest in Africa
nodes.description: A dormant stratovolcano. Three volcanic cones: Kibo, Mawenzi, Shira. Rising from the plains of Tanzania, it's the world's tallest free-standing mountain. Its glaciers are disappearing — climate backscatter.

nodes.label: Mount Elbrus — 5,642m — Highest in Europe
nodes.description: A dormant volcano in the Caucasus. Two summits (west: 5,642m, east: 5,621m). The European-Asian boundary runs through the Caucasus, making Elbrus's continental assignment debated.

nodes.label: Mount Vinson — 4,892m — Highest in Antarctica
nodes.description: In the Sentinel Range of the Ellsworth Mountains. Not discovered until 1958 (US Navy aerial survey). First climbed 1966. The loneliest high peak — surrounded by ice sheet.

nodes.label: Puncak Jaya (Carstensz Pyramid) — 4,884m — Highest in Oceania
nodes.description: The only one of the Seven Summits requiring technical rock climbing. Glaciers at the equator — rapidly disappearing. Located in Papua, Indonesia.

nodes.label: Mont Blanc — 4,810m — Highest in the Alps
nodes.description: First climbed 1786 — the birth of mountaineering. The Alps formed from the collision of the African and Eurasian plates. Mont Blanc is granite pushed up through limestone.

nodes.label: Matterhorn — 4,478m — The Icon
nodes.description: The most recognizable mountain silhouette on Earth. A horn peak — carved by glaciers from four sides. The Toblerone mountain. First ascent 1865, with 4 deaths on the descent.

nodes.label: Mount Rainier — 4,392m — Cascade Volcano
nodes.description: Active stratovolcano. Most glaciated peak in the contiguous US (26 major glaciers). Lahar hazard threatens Tacoma and Puyallup Valley. The Cascades are subduction volcanoes — Pacific Plate diving under North America.

nodes.label: Grand Teton — 4,199m — The Cathedral
nodes.description: The youngest mountains in the Rockies. A fault-block range — the Teton fault drops the valley (Jackson Hole) while lifting the peaks. No foothills — the mountains erupt directly from the plain. The backscatter of active faulting.

nodes.label: Mount Fuji — 3,776m — Sacred Symmetry
nodes.description: Near-perfect volcanic cone. Sacred in Shinto — one of Japan's Three Holy Mountains. Last erupted 1707. The most climbed mountain in the world (~300,000/year). Cultural backscatter as much as geological.

nodes.label: Mauna Kea — 4,207m (10,211m from ocean floor) — Tallest Mountain on Earth
nodes.description: Measured from its oceanic base, Mauna Kea is 10,211m — taller than Everest. A dormant shield volcano. Home to the world's largest astronomical observatory complex. Sacred to Native Hawaiians (Poliʻahu, goddess of snow).

nodes.label: Mammoth Cave — 685.6 km — Longest Cave on Earth
nodes.description: 685.6 km of surveyed passages (and counting — new passages found every year). Formed in Mississippian-age limestone over 10 million years. The Green River carved the master drain. The cave is the negative backscatter of water — the rock that's missing tells the story.

nodes.label: Sistema Ox Bel Ha — 541.8 km — Longest Underwater Cave
nodes.description: Underwater cave system in the Yucatan Peninsula. Connected to cenotes — natural sinkholes sacred to the Maya. The limestone platform of Yucatan is riddled with dissolved passages. Where the Maya met the underworld.

nodes.label: Suiyang Shuanghe Dongqun — 481.5 km — Longest Cave in Asia
nodes.description: In Guizhou Province. The longest cave in Asia and third longest globally. Multiple levels, formed in dolomite. Still actively being explored and extended.

nodes.label: Jewel Cave — 354.5 km — Third Longest in US
nodes.description: In the Black Hills of South Dakota. Named for calcite crystals lining its walls. Only 5% of estimated passages have been surveyed. The cave breathes — air pressure changes reveal enormous unsurveyed volume.

nodes.label: Krubera-Voronja Cave — 2,224m Deep — Deepest Cave on Earth (until 2024)
nodes.description: In the Arabika Massif, Western Caucasus. First cave to break 2,000m depth (2004). Held the depth record until Veryovkina surpassed its sump depth. The rock swallows you for over 2km straight down. Negative backscatter — the Earth opening its throat.

nodes.label: Veryovkina Cave — 2,209m Deep — Deepest Explored
nodes.description: Only 15m shallower than Krubera but the deepest continuous exploration. Same Arabika Massif. Named after Alexander Veryovkin. Explored by Russian and international teams pushing the limits of human underground endurance.

nodes.label: Hang Son Doong — 38.5M m³ — Largest Cave by Volume
nodes.description: Chambers 200m high, 150m wide. An underground river carved it. It has its own jungle, its own clouds, its own weather. A cave so large it has an ecosystem inside. The Earth hollowed out a cathedral and filled it with life.

nodes.label: Lechuguilla Cave — 245 km, 485m Deep — Most Beautiful Cave on Earth
nodes.description: Formed by sulfuric acid rising from below (not surface water). Contains rare minerals: selenite chandeliers, hydromagnesite balloons, subaqueous helictites. So pristine that NASA studies it as an analog for extraterrestrial life. Closed to the public — only scientific access.

nodes.label: Sistema Huautla — 1,560m Deep, 100.2 km — Deepest in Western Hemisphere
nodes.description: In the Sierra Mazateca, Oaxaca. Sacred to the Mazatec people. The deepest cave in the Americas. Requires underground camping for multi-week expeditions. Where the limestone mountains of Mexico open into vertical abysses.

nodes.label: Challenger Deep (Mariana Trench) — 10,924m — Deepest Point on Earth
nodes.description: The Pacific Plate dives beneath the Philippine Sea Plate. The ocean floor bends downward 10,924m — deeper than Everest is tall. Pressure: 1,086 atmospheres. Temperature: 1-4°C. Life exists here: amphipods, xenophyophores, shrimp. The Earth's deepest wound is still alive.

nodes.label: Horizon Deep (Tonga Trench) — 10,816m — Second Deepest
nodes.description: The Tonga Trench has the fastest convergence rate of any trench on Earth: 10.9 cm/year. The Pacific Plate is being consumed at maximum speed. The trench is the scar of maximum planetary violence.

nodes.label: Emden Deep (Philippine Trench) — 10,540m
nodes.description: Third deepest point on Earth. The Philippine Sea Plate subducts beneath the Eurasian Plate. Named after the German cruiser SMS Emden.

nodes.label: Kuril-Kamchatka Trench — 10,542m
nodes.description: Where the Pacific Plate dives under the Okhotsk Plate. The Kuril Islands volcanic arc sits above — every volcano is backscatter from the subduction below.

nodes.label: Kermadec Trench — 10,047m
nodes.description: North of New Zealand. Southern continuation of the Tonga Trench system. The same Pacific Plate subduction zone, different name.

nodes.label: Brownson Deep (Puerto Rico Trench) — 8,378m — Deepest in Atlantic
nodes.description: The deepest point in the Atlantic Ocean. The North American Plate and the Caribbean Plate meet here. The trench also marks a seismic hazard — tsunamis have hit the Caribbean from here.

nodes.label: Meteor Deep (South Sandwich Trench) — 8,265m
nodes.description: In the South Atlantic between South America and Antarctica. Named after the German research vessel Meteor. One of the most remote trenches on Earth.

nodes.label: Java Deep (Sunda Trench) — 7,187m — Deepest in Indian Ocean
nodes.description: The Australian Plate subducts beneath the Sunda Plate. This is the trench that generated the 2004 tsunami — the deadliest natural disaster of the 21st century. 230,000+ dead. The backscatter of this trench is measured in human lives.

nodes.label: Molloy Hole — 5,551m — Deepest in Arctic
nodes.description: Between Greenland and Svalbard. Not a subduction trench — it's on the Mid-Atlantic Ridge, where plates pull apart. The deepest point in the Arctic Ocean.

nodes.label: Grand Canyon National Park — 2 Billion Years of Earth's Story
nodes.description: The Colorado River carved a mile-deep, 277-mile-long canyon exposing 2 billion years of Earth's geological history. The oldest rocks (Vishnu Schist) are 1.8 billion years old. Each layer is a chapter. The canyon is the Earth's autobiography — written in stone, read by erosion.

nodes.label: Yellowstone National Park — The Supervolcano
nodes.description: First national park in the world (1872). Sits atop a supervolcano hotspot. 10,000+ thermal features including Old Faithful. The Yellowstone Caldera last erupted 640,000 years ago. The magma chamber is 80km long. The Earth is breathing here — every geyser is an exhale.

nodes.label: Yosemite National Park — Glacial Sculpture
nodes.description: Glaciers carved Half Dome, El Capitan, and Yosemite Falls from Sierra Nevada granite. Ansel Adams photographed it. John Muir fought for it. The granite is 100 million years old; the glacial carving is 2 million. The valley is backscatter from ice.

nodes.label: Grand Teton National Park — Fault-Block Cathedral
nodes.description: The Teton Range rises abruptly from the Jackson Hole valley — no foothills. The Teton fault drops the valley floor while lifting the mountains. 13,775 feet of vertical relief. The youngest mountains in the Rockies, still rising.

nodes.label: Denali National Park — 6 Million Acres of Wild
nodes.description: Home to North America's highest peak. 6 million acres — larger than Massachusetts. One road. Grizzlies, caribou, wolves, Dall sheep. The backscatter of genuine wilderness — the absence of human infrastructure IS the measurement.

nodes.label: Glacier National Park — Vanishing Ice
nodes.description: In 1850, there were 150 glaciers. In 2026, there are fewer than 25. Going-to-the-Sun Road crosses the Continental Divide. The park is climate backscatter — measuring the retreat of ice in real time.

nodes.label: Zion National Park — The Narrows
nodes.description: The North Fork of the Virgin River carved a 2,000-foot-deep canyon through Navajo Sandstone. The Narrows: 16 miles of hiking in the river, between walls 1,000 feet high and 20 feet apart. The backscatter of water through stone.

nodes.label: Arches National Park — 2,000+ Natural Arches
nodes.description: More natural stone arches than anywhere on Earth. Delicate Arch, Landscape Arch, Double Arch. Each one is entropy made beautiful — sandstone dissolving grain by grain until only the arch remains.

nodes.label: Bryce Canyon National Park — The Hoodoos
nodes.description: Not actually a canyon — a series of natural amphitheaters. Thousands of hoodoos (tall, thin rock spires). Frost wedging at 200+ freeze-thaw cycles per year. The hoodoos are backscatter from temperature — the stone cracking at the boundary between ice and water.

nodes.label: Death Valley National Park — Lowest, Hottest, Driest
nodes.description: Badwater Basin: 86m below sea level — lowest point in North America. Record: 56.7°C (134°F), 1913. Less than 5cm of rain per year. Sailing stones move across the playa. Extreme backscatter — the Earth at its harshest.

nodes.label: Everglades National Park — River of Grass
nodes.description: The only subtropical wilderness in the US. A 60-mile-wide, 100-mile-long shallow river flowing south through sawgrass. Home to Florida panthers, manatees, American crocodiles. Biological backscatter — the species tell you what the ecosystem is.

nodes.label: Hawaiʻi Volcanoes National Park — Where Earth Is Born
nodes.description: Kīlauea: one of the most active volcanoes on Earth. Mauna Loa: the largest shield volcano. The Hawaiian hotspot creates new land in real time. This is where the Earth's surface is being manufactured. Creation backscatter.

nodes.label: Redwood National Park — The Tallest Living Things
nodes.description: Coast redwoods (Sequoia sempervirens): tallest trees on Earth, up to 115.7m (379 ft). Some are 2,000+ years old. The trees predate the Roman Empire. Biological backscatter — 2,000 years of climate written in tree rings.

nodes.label: Sequoia National Park — The Largest Living Things
nodes.description: Giant sequoias (Sequoiadendron giganteum): largest trees by volume. General Sherman Tree: 52,500 cubic feet, ~2,200 years old. The biggest single organism on Earth. Volume backscatter — the space a single life can fill.

nodes.label: Carlsbad Caverns National Park — The Underground Cathedral
nodes.description: 119 known caves formed in a Permian reef. The Big Room: 8.2 acres, 78 stories tall. Every evening, 400,000 Brazilian free-tailed bats spiral out. Lechuguilla Cave is here — NASA's extraterrestrial life analog. Negative backscatter — the Earth removed rock and left wonder.

nodes.label: Mammoth Cave National Park — 685km of Passages
nodes.description: The longest known cave system on Earth. 685.6 km surveyed (and growing). 5 levels, 10 million years of dissolution. The Green River above, the cave below — same water, different timescales.

nodes.label: Acadia National Park — Where Mountains Meet the Sea
nodes.description: First national park east of the Mississippi. Cadillac Mountain: first place in the US to see sunrise from October to March. Granite mountains meeting the Atlantic. Where the continent ends.

nodes.label: Olympic National Park — Three Ecosystems in One
nodes.description: Temperate rainforest (Hoh: 12-14 feet of rain/year), alpine glaciers, and Pacific coast — all in one park. One of the most diverse parks in the US. Biodiversity backscatter — how many ways can life exist in one place?

nodes.label: Rocky Mountain National Park — Continental Divide
nodes.description: Trail Ridge Road: highest continuous paved road in US (12,183 ft). The Continental Divide splits the park — rain falling west goes to the Pacific, east goes to the Atlantic. The divide is the spine of the continent.

nodes.label: Great Smoky Mountains National Park — Most Visited Park
nodes.description: Most visited national park: 12.1 million visitors/year. Among the oldest mountains in the world (300 million years). More tree species than all of Northern Europe. The 'smoke' is actually isoprene from trees — biological exhaust. The forest breathes and you can see it.

nodes.label: Grand Canyon — Natural Wonder — 2 Billion Years Exposed
nodes.description: 277 miles long, 18 miles wide, 1 mile deep. The Colorado River exposed 2 billion years of geological history. 40 identified rock layers. Each layer is a chapter of Earth's autobiography. The canyon is the book. The river is the reader.

nodes.label: Great Barrier Reef — Natural Wonder — Largest Living Structure on Earth
nodes.description: 2,300 km long. Visible from space. 2,900 individual reefs, 900 islands. 1,500 species of fish, 400 types of coral. The largest single structure made by living organisms. Biological backscatter on a planetary scale. Bleaching events accelerating — climate backscatter.

nodes.label: Victoria Falls (Mosi-oa-Tunya) — Natural Wonder — The Smoke That Thunders
nodes.description: 1,708m wide, 108m tall. Largest sheet of falling water on Earth. The spray rises 400m and is visible from 50km away. Mosi-oa-Tunya: 'The Smoke That Thunders.' The Zambezi River drops over a basalt cliff into a chasm. The water is the backscatter. The thunder is the measurement.

nodes.label: Mount Everest — Natural Wonder — Roof of the World
nodes.description: 8,849m. The highest point on Earth's surface. Still rising 1cm/year as India pushes into Asia. Marine fossils at the summit — the rock that's now the highest on Earth was once ocean floor. The mountain is the backscatter of a 50-million-year collision.

nodes.label: Parícutin — Natural Wonder — The Volcano Born in a Cornfield
nodes.description: Born February 20, 1943 in a cornfield in Michoacán. Farmer Dionisio Pulido watched a crack open and lava emerge. Within a year, it was 336m tall. The only volcano whose entire lifecycle was witnessed by humans. It buried two villages. Creation and destruction in one measurement.

nodes.label: Harbour of Rio de Janeiro (Guanabara Bay) — Natural Wonder
nodes.description: Guanabara Bay: 412 km². Sugarloaf Mountain (Pão de Açúcar), Corcovado with Cristo Redentor. The Portuguese thought the bay was a river mouth — 'Rio de Janeiro' (River of January). The harbor is geological architecture — granite peaks surrounding tropical water.

nodes.label: Aurora Borealis / Australis — Natural Wonder — The Sky on Fire
nodes.description: Solar wind particles follow Earth's magnetic field lines to the poles, collide with atmospheric gases, and emit light. Green (oxygen at 100-300km), red (oxygen above 300km), purple/blue (nitrogen). The aurora is backscatter from the sun — Earth's magnetic field revealing itself by catching particles from 150 million km away.
nodes.note: Coordinates approximate — visible across polar regions

nodes.label: KARST — The Dissolution Bridge Between Peaks and Caves
nodes.description: Karst: slightly acidic water (CO₂ + H₂O → carbonic acid) dissolves limestone over millions of years. Tectonic uplift raises ancient seabeds into mountains. Water infiltrates from peak to bedrock. The cave is the NEGATIVE of the mountain — what was removed below is what stands above. Every cave passage is a measurement of water, time, and rock chemistry. The peak pushes up; the cave dissolves down. Same stone, opposite sign.

nodes.label: THE WATER CYCLE — Agent of All Vertical Sculpture
nodes.description: Rain falls on peaks, becomes rivers that carve canyons, infiltrates limestone to dissolve caves, flows to the ocean, evaporates, returns to peaks. The same water molecule that erodes the Grand Canyon could have dissolved a passage in Mammoth Cave 10,000 years earlier. Water is the universal agent — it carves from above (erosion), dissolves from within (karst), and subducts with ocean plates. The water cycle IS the backscatter cycle.

nodes.label: RING OF FIRE — Pacific Tectonic Loop
nodes.description: 40,000 km horseshoe of oceanic trenches, volcanic arcs, and seismic belts. 75% of Earth's active volcanoes. 90% of earthquakes. The same subduction that pulls trenches DOWN pushes volcanic mountains UP. Fuji, Rainier, Denali, Aconcagua — all Ring of Fire peaks. Mariana, Tonga, Kuril, Kermadec — all Ring of Fire trenches. The ring connects peaks and trenches as CAUSE and EFFECT of the same plate motion.

nodes.label: SUBDUCTION — One Plate Dives, Another Rises
nodes.description: When oceanic crust meets continental crust, the denser ocean plate dives under. Downward: trench forms. Upward: volcanic arc rises. The limestone on the ocean floor gets scraped off, uplifted, and eventually dissolved by rain into caves. Subduction is the engine that connects ALL three: trenches (where the plate goes down), mountains (where magma comes up), caves (where uplifted limestone dissolves). One process, three signatures.

nodes.label: EARTH'S VERTICAL ENVELOPE — 21,148m of Relief
nodes.description: From Challenger Deep (-10,924m) through sea level (0m) through Krubera Cave (surface to -2,224m below the Caucasus) to Everest (+8,849m) to Mauna Kea measured from ocean floor (+10,211m). The Earth's total vertical dynamic range: 21,135m from deepest ocean to highest peak above sea level. But measured from Mauna Kea's base to Challenger Deep: 21,148m. Every point on this axis is a measurement the planet made of itself.

Caucasus: peak at +5,642m, cave at -2,224m. 7,866m vertical range. Same tectonic uplift raised the peak AND exposed the limestone that dissolved into the deepest cave on Earth.
Same Caucasus collision. Mountain rises; water descends. Both are backscatter from the Arabian-Eurasian plate boundary.
Rocky Mountain uplift exposed Black Hills Paleozoic limestone. Same continental deformation — Laramide orogeny pushed mountains up, exposed ancient seabeds to dissolution below.
Carlsbad Permian reef was once ocean floor like the marine fossils atop Aconcagua. Both were seabed, both were uplifted. One became a mountain, one became a cave.
Both Americas subduction. Nazca plate dives under South America → Andes. Cocos plate dives under Mexico → Sierra Mazateca with cave system below.
Same India-Asia collision zone. Himalayas pushed UP, Southeast Asian karst plateaus dissolved DOWN. Tethys Sea limestone became both the highest mountains and the largest caves.
Pacific Plate subduction creates BOTH: Mariana Trench pulls the plate DOWN, Japanese volcanic arc pushes magma UP. Same plate motion, opposite sign. Fuji is Challenger Deep's backscatter.
Cascadia subduction: Juan de Fuca plate dives under North America. Trench offshore, volcanic arc onshore. Rainier IS the trench's echo on land.
Both Pacific rim. Nazca→Andes pushes Aconcagua UP. Pacific→Tonga pushes Horizon Deep DOWN. The ring of fire connects them.
Same Pacific Ring of Fire. Kuril subduction and Japanese volcanic arc — adjacent segments of the same tectonic circle.
Alaska Range from Pacific plate subduction. Same plate whose other edge dives into the Mariana Trench. One plate, two signatures: a mountain in Alaska, a trench in Micronesia.
Carbonic acid + Mississippian limestone + 10M years = 685.6 km of passages. The longest negentropy on Earth.
Karst dissolution in Caucasus limestone. 2,224m of vertical cave = 2,224m of rock removed grain by grain.
Karst in Phong Nha-Kẻ Bàng limestone plateau. Volume large enough for its own weather system.
Yucatan Platform karst. Cenotes = collapsed cave ceilings. The Maya knew these as entrances to Xibalba.
NOT carbonic acid — SULFURIC acid from below. H₂S rose from oil deposits, oxidized to H₂SO₄, dissolved limestone from underneath. Caves carved upward, not downward.
The Grand Canyon walls contain dozens of caves. The Colorado River carved the canyon; karst dissolved caves within its walls. Same limestone, two processes.
Zion's Narrows = surface karst. Water carved a slot canyon through sandstone. Cave formation in miniature, open to the sky.
Water IS the karst agent. Rain → CO₂ absorption → carbonic acid → limestone dissolution → cave. Without water, no caves.
Colorado River carved 277 miles, 1 mile deep. Water is the reader of the Earth's autobiography.
Zambezi River at maximum spectacle. Surface water made visible. The falls ARE the water cycle pausing to be measured.
Glaciers = water frozen in transit. The retreat of ice is the water cycle accelerating.
Glacial carving in granite. Water as ice sculpted Half Dome and El Capitan. Yosemite Falls: the water cycle still performing.
Philippine Sea plate subduction → Japanese volcanic arc → Fuji
Juan de Fuca plate subduction → Cascade volcanic arc → Rainier
Nazca plate subduction → Andes → highest peak in Americas
Pacific plate subduction → Alaska Range → highest peak in N. America
Pacific-Philippine convergence → deepest point on Earth
Pacific-Tonga convergence → fastest subduction, second deepest
Pacific-Okhotsk convergence → volcanic Kuril Islands above
Indo-Australian subduction → 2004 tsunami. The ring's deadliest backscatter.
Subduction IS the ring of fire. Every trench is a subduction zone. Every volcanic arc sits above one.
Subduction uplifts ancient ocean floor limestone onto continental surfaces. Rain dissolves it into caves. Without subduction, no uplifted limestone, no caves.
Lower boundary: -10,924m below sea level
Upper boundary: +8,849m above sea level
Interior measurement: 2,224m of vertical cave = the deepest humans have gone INSIDE the Earth
True tallest: 10,211m base-to-peak, but 6,004m is underwater. The ocean hides half the mountain.
Badwater Basin: -86m. Lowest dry land in N. America. A valley so deep it sinks below the sea.
